description: I'm a space enthusiast with a background in Physics and Computer Science, research experience, and a passion for creative exploration. I enjoy bringing diverse perspectives together, thinking outside the box, and turning interesting ideas into reality. Looking for enthusiastic, curious and collaborative teammates with skills in coding, data science, engineering, design, or creative technology. Most importantly, I value initiative, fresh thinking and a willingness to experiment.
summary:
What we developed: EARTHSONIC, a free, keyboard-friendly web app and listening game that turns real Earth data into sound, plus five original tracks our team composed from those sonifications (earthquakes, oceans, heatwaves, wildfires and air pollution).

How it addresses the challenge: The Earth Information Jukebox asks for new ways to experience Earth information. EARTHSONIC maps each data series to pitch and pulse speed, so players hear an earthquake, an ocean current or a smog spike, find its peak by ear, and then check the real numbers. Blindfold Mode makes a full round playable without sight.

Why it matters: Earth science mostly reaches people as charts and maps, which leave out the 2.2 billion people living with vision impairment and feel abstract to many others, including children and non-technical audiences. Sound adds another way in: it complements visuals rather than replacing them, and makes environmental change something people can feel and remember.
details:
EARTHSONIC: Hear the Planet Change
Real Earth data, turned into sound you can play, guess and feel.

1. THE PROBLEM
Most Earth science reaches the public through maps, charts and colour scales. For people who can't see them, these formats are hard or impossible to use, and for children and non-technical audiences they often feel abstract.
According to the World Health Organization's World Report on Vision (2019), at least 2.2 billion people live with some form of vision impairment. When Earth information is shared only visually, a large part of the world is left out.

2. WHAT EARTHSONIC DOES
EARTHSONIC is a free, keyboard-friendly web app and interactive listening game. Each mission turns a real data series into sound using two mappings:

  • Pitch
  • Pulse speed

Players scrub through time, listen to the data, find the peak by ear, and then reveal the real values and the science behind them.

Interactive Earth and accessibility

  • A 3D Earth built with NASA Blue Marble imagery gives each event its geographic context, with day and night shading calculated from the Sun's position.
  • Blindfold Mode hides the screen and adds narration, so a full round can be played with sound and keyboard alone.
  • Every control is keyboard-accessible.

3. HOW IT WORKS: FROM DATA TO MUSIC

  • Step 1, Data to tone (scientific sonification): each data series is rescaled to 0–1 and mapped to pitch and pulse rate, giving a faithful audio picture of the measurements.
  • Step 2, Tone to music (human creativity): our team used these sonifications as the starting point for five original compositions, built with melody, harmony, rhythm, sampling and sound design. Wherever possible, they keep the original timelines and dynamic shape.
  • Step 3, Play and learn: players listen for patterns, guess the peak, then compare their answer with the real values and the explanation.

4. BENEFITS

  • Students and non-technical audiences: a hands-on way to understand graphs, peaks and trends before the maths.
  • Universities and educators: a ready teaching resource linking science, music and technology.
  • Scientists and researchers: listening may help spot changes or anomalies. This is a potential use that still needs testing.
  • People with visual impairments: a way to explore environmental data without relying only on graphs. It complements visual tools rather than being a complete accessibility solution.
  • General public: free, browser-based, no login, and works with just a keyboard and headphones.

5. INTENDED IMPACT
Our goal is to make Earth information something people can hear, experience and remember. EARTHSONIC aims to:

  • give teachers and learners a free tool that works with or without sight;
  • spark interest in climate science through interactive discovery;
  • make scientific data approachable for non-technical audiences;
  • explore how science, sound and human creativity connect.

Because sometimes, the best way to understand the world is to listen to it.

6. FUTURE WORK (planned, not yet built)

  • Musical variations: new instruments and styles for the same dataset, all reviewed by human creators.
  • New sonification models: for more graph types, including terrain and geography for visually impaired users.
  • Educational resources: classroom kits and teacher guides.
  • More NASA datasets: additional Earth-observation data and phenomena.

7. TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGY

  • Web app: HTML, CSS, JavaScript, the Web Audio API for live sound, and a 3D globe renderer.
  • Data and audio processing: Python, NumPy, SciPy.
  • Demo and presentation: Playwright, Pillow, FFmpeg, python-pptx, LibreOffice.
  • Hosting: Vercel, at earth-sonic.com and earthsonic-echoquest.vercel.app.
  • Music: five original tracks composed, performed, mixed and mastered by team members.
  • Narration: the demo video's voice is synthetic, generated with Microsoft Edge text-to-speech.

8. HOW OUR PROJECT IS CREATIVE

  1. Science becomes a game: instead of reading a chart, players listen, guess the peak, and then discover the real numbers.
  2. Two layers of sound: code-generated sonification that maps the data faithfully, plus human-composed music that interprets the same events emotionally.
  3. Found sounds and voice: percussion recorded on books and tables, a team member's voice used as an instrument, and metaphors such as an unanswered telephone and a heartbeat fading to a flatline.
  4. Accessibility by design: Blindfold Mode turns the whole experience into an audio-first game.

9. FACTORS THE TEAM CONSIDERED

  • Scientific integrity: the data-to-sound mapping stays unchanged under the music. Real values are revealed after each guess, and every dataset is credited.
  • Transparency: we clearly separate live features from future ideas, NASA data from other open data, and code-generated sonification from human music.
  • Accessibility: full keyboard control, narration, Blindfold Mode, and two sound cues (pitch and pulse speed), so no single characteristic carries the meaning.
  • Listening comfort: a 150–880 Hz range and controlled loudness, for both laptop speakers and headphones.
  • Usability and reach: free, browser-based, no login, quick to load.
  • Rights and branding: original team-made music and sound effects, no third-party samples, openly licensed fonts, credited open datasets. No NASA branding is used and no NASA endorsement is implied.
  • Constraints: built in a 48-hour window. We acknowledge that the final mixes have some limits in frequency balance and polish.

10. ARTISTIC INTERPRETATION AND STORYTELLING
We brought an artist and a professional music producer into the team to go beyond converting data into sound. Using the sonifications as raw material, we created five original tracks:

  • Earthquakes: built on drum sounds sampled from the sonification. Heavy patterns and rising tension aim to make you feel the vibration in your chest. It is deliberately unsettling, not pleasant.
  • Oceans: layered synthesizers from the original sonification create a vast, flowing soundscape. Arpeggiated vocal samples and percussion played on books and tables give it organic, tidal textures.
  • Heatwaves: an A–B structure that moves from a gentle melody into something increasingly intense. A telephone that keeps ringing, unanswered, stands for an escalating warning nobody responds to.
  • Wildfires: a nostalgic chant calling home to a place that no longer exists, for the people and animals who lost their habitats. The final note stays unresolved, an attempt to return to what was lost.
  • Air Pollution: dark and haunting. A pulsing beep like a heartbeat slowly leads to a flatline, showing what inaction could cost.

Artistic approach: these tracks are interpretations of the sonifications, not exact mappings. Wherever possible they keep the original timelines and loudness changes, so the music stays tied to the science. The musical work was led by the team's artist and producer, who also mixed and mastered within the 48-hour window.

11. LIMITATIONS

  • The 48-hour timeline didn't allow user testing with our target audiences, especially people with visual impairments.
  • We built in keyboard navigation, narration and Blindfold Mode, but testing with real users is our first next step to find gaps and improve the experience beyond what currently exists.
